Chapter 7: Accountability, Justice, and the Limits of the System
When someone’s been hurt, the question of accountability comes front and center, doesn’t it? What does justice really look like in a world where so many survivors—people just trying to be heard—end up disbelieved, dismissed, or even retraumatized by the very systems that are supposed to protect them?
The stories here dive into just how complicated seeking justice can be. Sometimes it’s through official channels, like courts or campus authorities. Other times, it’s through more personal, even community-driven paths.
Picture this: A college student, after months of wrestling with her decision, finally chooses to report her assault to campus officials. She gathers evidence, braces herself for the hard questions, and steps into a process that quickly turns slow and tangled in red tape. There are delays, skepticism—so much second-guessing. In the end, the outcome barely feels like justice: a mild consequence for the perpetrator, and for her, a sense of exposure that just won’t go away. She’s left wondering... did any of it really change anything?
Then there’s another story—a man who, years after causing harm as a young person, reaches out to seek forgiveness. The conversation is tough, awkward, full of apologies and explanations. The person he hurt? They’re not sure how to respond. There’s no tidy ending, no grand moment of closure. It becomes clear that accountability isn’t just about punishment; it’s about really acknowledging the harm, taking true responsibility, and, wherever possible, trying to make amends.
You’ll hear about a community organizer, too—someone who’s just fed up with how the legal system keeps letting people down. So, they help start a restorative justice circle. Survivors and those who’ve caused harm sit down together, talk, listen, and try to really understand each other. The process is far from perfect—sometimes it’s uncomfortable, even messy. But for some, it’s the first time they actually feel heard.
Most people don’t realize just how limited the options for justice can be. Our legal system? It often struggles to handle the messy, deeply personal realities of sexual violence. It’s built to focus on evidence and intent—things that don’t always capture the impact or help people heal. That’s why so many survivors choose not to report what happened at all—they’re scared of not being believed or facing backlash. And even when their stories are taken seriously, the process can end up retraumatizing them.
What these stories make clear is that justice isn’t one-size-fits-all. For some, it’s about seeing the person who hurt them held accountable in court. For others, it’s about finally being believed, having their pain acknowledged, or just finding a way to move forward—no judge or jury involved. We all want justice, but the path to get there? It’s as individual as each person’s story.
By looking closely at different ways to find accountability, these stories challenge the idea that punishment is the only—or even the best—way to respond to harm. They ask us to imagine new possibilities for healing, for repair, even for transformation.
The work isn’t finished—and the answers are rarely simple. But being willing to ask tough questions, to listen with an open heart, and to seek justice in all its forms? That’s a key part of challenging rape culture and building something better.
